tldr: We propose "EgoX," a framework that organizes functionally corresponding observation and action modalities across radically different data sources—humans, real robots (humanoids, quadrupeds, wheeled bimanual systems, etc.), and simulators—to pretrain a shared Transformer. By introducing "Embodiment Dreaming," which predicts future latent states during training, EgoX substantially boosts task progress on unseen environments and novel objects.
hero_caption: Overall framework of EgoX. Egocentric (first-person) demonstrations collected from highly diverse embodiments—including humans, humanoids, quadrupeds, wheeled bimanual robots, tabletop arms, and simulators—are pooled for pretraining and then adapted to target robots. EgoX achieves strong generalization via a shared Transformer trunk, embodiment-specific modules, and a Dream Expert that predicts future embodiment states.
overview:
When teaching robots to perform a wide variety of manipulation tasks dexterously, it would be ideal to leverage the vast amounts of manipulation data gathered by humans, other robots, and simulators. In practice, however, robots differ in arm degrees of freedom, camera placement, and end-effector design (dexterous multi-finger hands, parallel-jaw grippers, fixed tools, etc.). This "embodiment gap" makes it extremely difficult to simply mix diverse datasets together for training.

To address this challenge, the authors introduce the EgoX learning framework. Their core insight is that "while overall morphologies differ, localized body parts such as wrists, end-effectors, and torsos fulfill functionally corresponding roles." EgoX decomposes all observations and actions into semantic modalities defined in first-person (egocentric) coordinate frames. It processes them through an architecture (MXT+) that pairs embodiment-specific tokenizers and action decoders with a single shared Transformer trunk. Furthermore, EgoX incorporates "Embodiment Dreaming"—an auxiliary training objective that predicts future latent features—so the policy's internal representations learn the underlying dynamics of "how its own body will move next."

In evaluations across six robot embodiments (five physical robots and one simulated humanoid) alongside human data, EgoX was tested on five manipulation tasks spanning 13 task–embodiment pairs. Cross-embodiment pretraining improved average normalized task progress from 0.63 to 0.80 compared to training from scratch. The performance gain was especially striking in challenging out-of-distribution (OOD) settings involving novel objects and unseen configurations, where progress jumped from 0.53 to 0.77, demonstrating that pretraining across embodiments dramatically strengthens a robot's adaptability.
contributions: Established a unified representation pipeline aligning human, diverse real robot, and simulator data using functionally and anatomically corresponding modalities (wrists, end-effector keypoints, torsos, etc.) grounded in egocentric reference frames.
Introduced MXT+, a modularized architecture combining per-modality I/O interfaces with a shared Transformer trunk, which absorbs embodiment-specific differences while transferring shared skills.

Formulated the training-only "Embodiment Dreaming" objective, predicting latent representations of future visual and proprioceptive states to imprint each embodiment's dynamics onto the shared trunk without heavy pixel reconstruction.

Conducted extensive experiments across 13 task–embodiment pairs spanning five physical robots and one simulator, demonstrating that pretraining and dreaming deliver substantial performance gains, especially under out-of-distribution (OOD) conditions.

sections.heading: Bridging the embodiment gap: Aligning viewpoints and modalities
sections.summary: Just as in NLP and computer vision, robotics seeks generalist models learned from diverse data. However, differences in morphology, sensing, and control interfaces have posed a major hurdle. This paper treats humans, real robots, and simulators as peers under unified modal representations and latent dynamics prediction (dreaming) to overcome this barrier.
sections.details:
Spurred by the success of foundation models, robotics is actively pursuing generalist policies capable of adapting across varied environments and tasks. Future deployments will likely see tabletop arms, wheeled mobile manipulators, humanoids, and quadrupeds coexisting, each suited to different roles. Training each robot platform in isolation incurs prohibitive data collection costs.

Available data sources include egocentric human video, teleoperation logs from diverse robots, and scalable simulation. While these sources are complementary, their morphologies, viewpoints, proprioceptive states, and action spaces are radically heterogeneous.

To tackle this discrepancy, the authors established a core design principle: transfer should occur across semantically corresponding modalities, while keeping individual sensing and control interfaces modularized for each embodiment. This is the foundation of EgoX. It consists of three primary components:

- Data alignment through a unified egocentric coordinate system and modularized modalities
- MXT+, a Transformer combining embodiment-specific tokenizers/experts with a shared trunk
- Embodiment Dreaming, an auxiliary objective predicting future latent states to learn physical dynamics

Across 13 task–embodiment pairs spanning five physical robots and one simulator, cross-embodiment pretraining boosted average normalized task progress from 0.63 to 0.80 compared to training from scratch. In out-of-distribution (OOD) scenarios, progress surged from 0.53 to 0.77, underscoring the strong transfer benefits of heterogeneous pretraining.

captions.F2: Example of shared task structure across heterogeneous embodiments. In the "Kitchen-Bread" task (spreading sauce on bread), a human (Human-Dex5), a real humanoid (G1-Dex5), a simulated humanoid (G1-Sim-Dex3), and a wheeled bimanual robot (R1Lite-Gripper) share the same functional stages (reaching, carrying, spreading), despite their radically different morphologies.

sections.heading: At the crossroads of cross-embodiment learning and world models
sections.summary: While policy sharing across different robots and learning from human egocentric video are active areas of research, handling broad morphological differences remains difficult. World models that predict future states have also gained traction. EgoX stands out by uniting diverse embodiments—from dexterous hands to rigid tools—through a modular design that integrates action generation with latent dynamics prediction.
sections.details:
### Current Landscape of Cross-Embodiment Learning
Efforts to share manipulation policies across different robots (such as Open X-Embodiment and Octo) are expanding. However, many prior works remain limited to manipulators with comparable degrees of freedom, or simply append embodiment-specific heads without facilitating deeper, modality-level sharing. EgoX embraces a much wider spectrum of morphological diversity, spanning humanoids, wheeled bimanual platforms, tabletop arms, quadrupeds, 3- to 5-finger dexterous hands, parallel-jaw grippers, and rigid tools.

### Leveraging Egocentric Human Data
With the proliferation of XR headsets and smart glasses, extracting manipulation skills from first-person human video has gained substantial interest. However, most existing approaches focus on mapping human motion onto a single specific target robot. EgoX treats humans and robots symmetrically as peer embodiments, pretraining a shared representation across all data simultaneously.

### World Action Models and Embodiment Modeling
World action models that predict future observations (pixels or features) alongside actions provide a powerful framework for representation learning. EgoX's "Embodiment Dreaming" adopts a JEPA-style (Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture) formulation to predict future latent states of proprioception and visual features. By avoiding expensive pixel-level reconstruction, it effectively teaches each embodiment's physical dynamics to the shared Transformer backbone.

sections.heading: Embodiment-specific modules meet a dreaming Transformer trunk
sections.summary: EgoX structures modalities within a unified egocentric coordinate frame, combining embodiment-specific tokenizers and action experts with a shared Transformer trunk (MXT+). During training, an auxiliary "Embodiment Dreaming" objective predicts future latent body states, efficiently modeling each robot's dynamics without pixel-level reconstruction.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Egocentric Cross-Embodiment Data Representation
Even when full-body morphologies differ, localized body parts share functional roles. EgoX decomposes observations and actions into functional modalities and expresses them within standardized reference frames:
- Root frame ($\mathcal{F}_{\text{root}}$): Ground projection of the feet or base, representing torso pose and base velocity commands.
- Egocentric frame ($\mathcal{F}_{\text{ego}}$): Centered at the primary camera, representing left and right wrist poses ($\bm{x}_{\mathrm{L}}, \bm{x}_{\mathrm{R}}$).
- Wrist frame ($\mathcal{F}_{\text{wrist}}$): Anchored at the wrist, expressing "end-effector keypoints" ($\bm{p}_{\mathrm{L}}, \bm{p}_{\mathrm{R}}$) at fingertips or tool tips.
By adopting 3D end-effector keypoints instead of raw joint angles, diverse end-effectors—such as 5-finger hands, 2-finger grippers, and fixed tools—are described within a shared geometric space.

### 3.2 Modularized Cross-Embodiment Transformer (MXT+)
Each observation modality uses a dedicated tokenizer $\phi^e_m$. Image inputs are processed by a shared vision backbone coupled with embodiment-specific cross-attention, while poses and joint states are tokenized via MLPs. These tokens are concatenated and passed into a shared encoder-decoder Transformer trunk $G_\theta$. From the trunk outputs, embodiment-specific action experts $\psi^e_m$ predict action chunks spanning a future horizon $H$.

### 3.3 Embodiment Dreaming (Latent State Prediction)
Standard behavioral cloning lacks awareness of how actions alter future embodiment states. EgoX introduces a Dream Expert $\psi^e_{\mathrm{dream}}$ to predict future latent features $\bm{Y}^{e}_{t+k}$ at horizons $k \in \{20, 40, 60\}$ (corresponding to 0.66–2.0 seconds ahead) from current body tokens.
Prediction targets are generated using an exponential moving average (EMA) copy of the encoder with stop-gradient applied. The loss combines cosine similarity and norm-matching terms. This predictive branch is active only during training, incurring zero computational overhead during inference.

### 3.4 Pretraining and Adaptation (Fine-Tuning)
Training follows a two-stage paradigm. First, MXT+ is pretrained by uniformly sampling across all data (humans, other robots, and simulation) excluding the target task and target robot. Next, the shared trunk and embodiment-specific modules are fine-tuned on a small set of demonstrations collected on the target robot.

captions.F3: Model architecture of MXT+. Top left: Embodiment-specific tokenizers map various observation modalities into a unified token space, processed by the shared Transformer trunk in the center. Top right: Dedicated action experts output action chunks, while the purple Dream Expert predicts future latent features from an EMA teacher. Bottom: The six robot embodiments and human hand configurations supported by the framework.
captions.F4: Conceptual diagram of unified egocentric coordinate frames and token spaces. Torsos are anchored in the root frame ($\mathcal{F}_{\text{root}}$), wrists in the camera egocentric frame ($\mathcal{F}_{\text{ego}}$), and end-effector keypoints in the wrist frame ($\mathcal{F}_{\text{wrist}}$). These provide geometrically consistent semantic tokens to the shared trunk regardless of morphological differences.

sections.heading: Evaluating transfer performance across six embodiments and unseen settings
sections.summary: EgoX was evaluated across 13 task–embodiment pairs spanning five physical robots (humanoids, quadrupeds, wheeled bimanual, and tabletop arms) and one simulator. Cross-embodiment pretraining improved average task progress from 0.63 to 0.80 over training from scratch, jumping from 0.53 to 0.77 in out-of-distribution settings. Ablations validate the modular design, the dreaming objective, and improved latent geometry alignment.
sections.details:
### Experimental Setup
Evaluations covered 13 pairs spanning five tasks (spreading sauce on bread, wiping, block sorting, T-block insertion, and cat litter scooping) and six robot embodiments (G1-Dex5, xArm7-Dex4, G1-Sim-Dex3, LocoMan-Dex2, R1Lite-Gripper, and Z1-Tool). EgoX was benchmarked against ACT, the $\pi_{0.5}$ VLA model, and MXT+ trained from scratch. Experiments evaluated both in-distribution (ID) conditions matching training demonstrations and out-of-distribution (OOD) conditions with novel objects and unseen layouts, measuring normalized task progress.

### Benefits of Pretraining
Pretrained MXT+ outperformed all baselines in 12 out of 13 pairs, lifting overall average task progress from 0.63 (from scratch) to 0.80. The gain was particularly pronounced under OOD conditions, rising from 0.53 to 0.77 (with dramatic gains on tasks like G1-Dex5 block insertion and Z1-Tool litter scooping). This confirms that cross-embodiment experience provides a robust manipulation prior for unfamiliar situations.

### Expanding Pretraining Data and Ablations
The authors varied the pretraining mixture: None, Human-only, Human + other robots, and All-data (including target embodiment data from other tasks). Human data alone boosted OOD robustness, while adding robot data improved ID performance. Downstream success scaled consistently as the pretraining mixture grew broader.

### Role of Embodiment Dreaming and Modular Design
Comparing MXT+ against a variant without dreaming (MXT), MXT+ achieved superior performance across all seven evaluated setups, improving average task progress from 0.63 to 0.78. In comparisons with a "Coarse" baseline that merges observations into an unseparated body token, MXT+'s fine-grained modularization proved far superior on complex tasks combining locomotion and arm manipulation.

### Latent Space Geometric Analysis
Using Gromov-Wasserstein (GW) discrepancy, the authors quantified geometric alignment in the shared trunk's latent representations across embodiments. Pretraining reduced cross-embodiment GW distance by an average of 21.30%, and adding Embodiment Dreaming reduced it by 38.52%. This quantitatively confirms that dreaming aligns the underlying task structure within the latent space across differing physical forms.

captions.F5: Manipulation performance across 13 task–embodiment pairs. Bars show normalized task progress for ACT, $\pi_{0.5}$, MXT+ from scratch, and pretrained MXT+. Pretrained MXT+ (dark orange) consistently outperforms baselines across almost all settings, with especially large margins in OOD evaluations (light bars).
captions.F9: Percentage change in Gromov-Wasserstein (GW) discrepancy across embodiment pairs. Bottom-left (red) reflects changes from pretraining; top-right (purple) reflects changes from Embodiment Dreaming. Negative values indicate tighter geometric alignment, showing that dreaming consistently aligns representation geometry across all pairs.

sections.heading: Separating shared intelligence from modular control
sections.summary: EgoX demonstrates strong transfer capability by structuring human, robot, and simulation data into functional modalities and modeling dynamics via Embodiment Dreaming. Future directions include scaling dataset size, automating coordinate frame configuration, and resolving data imbalances across platforms.
sections.details:
This work demonstrates that agents with vastly different physical bodies can share manipulation experience within a unified model when provided with egocentric modal alignment and a latent dynamics prediction task. By decoupling low-level sensing and control into modular interfaces while integrating high-level task representations in a shared Transformer trunk, EgoX outlines a promising architectural direction for generalist robot foundation models.

The authors note several limitations and avenues for future work:
- Dataset scale: Experiments relied on data collected within their research setup, leaving evaluation on web-scale datasets to future exploration.
- Manual configuration: Integrating a new robot currently requires manually defining modality mappings and coordinate transformation matrices.
- Data imbalance: Demonstration volume varies widely across platforms (e.g., smaller datasets for the quadrupedal LocoMan), which can lead to overfitting when sampling mini-batches uniformly.

Future work will focus on automated modality discovery and sampling strategies tailored to data diversity.

sections.heading: Appendix: Handling missing modalities and the execution pipeline
sections.summary: The appendix details how the framework handles embodiments lacking specific components—such as single-arm robots or rigid tools—and explains the end-to-end pipeline from Vision Pro teleoperation to low-level robot control (50 Hz to 400 Hz).
sections.details:
### Flexible Handling of Missing Modalities
Single-arm robots lack left-arm and left-wrist inputs, and simple grippers lack the multi-joint degrees of freedom of dexterous hands. MXT+ defines availability indicators $\delta^e_m$ for each modality. Absent observation modalities are either omitted from the token sequence or substituted with zero tokens. Losses corresponding to missing action modalities are masked out during optimization, allowing arbitrary embodiment configurations to interface smoothly with the same shared Transformer trunk.

### Data Collection and Execution Pipeline
Human demonstrations and robot teleoperation were collected using Apple Vision Pro (and PICO 4 Ultra) headsets, recording stereo camera video and hand poses at 30 Hz. Predicted action chunks from MXT+ are interpolated and dispatched to low-level controllers operating at platform-native control frequencies (50 Hz for G1, 200 Hz for R1Lite, and 400 Hz for xArm7 and Z1), ensuring smooth physical execution.

captions.F11: Overview of the pipeline from demonstration capture to unified representation and physical execution. Movements recorded via Vision Pro headsets are converted into standardized pose and action trajectories at 30 Hz. Action chunks generated by MXT+ are then executed by low-level controllers running between 50 Hz and 400 Hz across target robots.

takeaways: Representing action spaces as end-effector keypoints in unified egocentric frames (camera-relative and wrist-relative) enables cross-embodiment data sharing across multi-finger hands, parallel grippers, and rigid tools without relying on joint angles.

Embodiment Dreaming provides a training-only latent state prediction objective that imprints physical dynamics into the shared backbone without the computational cost of pixel reconstruction or inference overhead.
Pretraining on diverse mixtures of human and heterogeneous robot data substantially boosts policy adaptability in out-of-distribution (OOD) settings, raising task progress from 0.53 to 0.77.

Modulating inputs and outputs into dedicated modules for wrists, hands, torsos, and mobile bases—rather than a single coarse whole-body tokenizer—is critical for preventing negative transfer on complex manipulation tasks involving locomotion.
limitations: Adding a new robot or tool requires manually defining end-effector keypoints and setting up transformation matrices.
When datasets are imbalanced across embodiments, uniform sampling across platforms can lead to overfitting on embodiments with limited demonstration counts.
Simulation experiments were restricted to a single humanoid platform on two kitchen tasks, leaving large-scale Sim-to-Real co-training to future studies.
